Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise, and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, and health.
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976 introduced Fundamental Duties under Article 51A, including respecting the National Flag and National Anthem.
The Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) case established that standing respectfully without singing the national anthem does not constitute disrespect, protecting religious and conscientious objectors.
The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 penalizes intentional disrespect or active prevention of the singing of the National Anthem.

texts.x: General Studies-2; Topic: Indian Constitution– historical underpinnings, evolution, features, amendments, significant provisions and basic structure. Introduction The Supreme Court examined the constitutional validity of penal provisions concerning the mandatory singing of Vande Mataram, focusing on whether conscientious objection can invite criminal prosecution. The Court held that individuals cannot be penalized for declining to sing the National …

points: The Supreme Court examined the constitutional validity of penal provisions concerning the mandatory singing of Vande Mataram, focusing on whether conscientious objection can invite criminal prosecution.
The Court held that individuals cannot be penalized for declining to sing the National Song if it conflicts with their conscience or religious faith, provided they maintain a respectful posture.
The Court distinguished between the executive power to notify official songs and its own duty to safeguard citizens from punitive overreach and constitutional rights violations.
Article 19(1)(a) protects free expression, including the negative right not to speak or sing against one's will.
Article 25 protects freedom of conscience, recognizing that singing verses invoking deities may conflict with certain theological beliefs.
Article 21 and the K.S. Puttaswamy judgment establish that personal privacy encompasses mental autonomy, barring the state from forcibly extracting ideological allegiance.
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment consciously omitted the National Song from Article 51A(a) on Fundamental Duties, differentiating it from the National Anthem.
Criminalizing silent non-compliance fails the minimal impairment test of rights, making criminal penalties disproportionate to the state's civic objectives.
National cohesion should be anchored in constitutional values of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity rather than ceremonial conformity.
sum.text:
The Supreme Court examined the constitutional validity of penal provisions concerning the mandatory singing of Vande Mataram , focusing on whether conscientious objection can invite criminal prosecution.
The Court held that individuals cannot be penalized for declining to sing the National Song if it conflicts with their conscience or religious faith, provided they maintain a respectful posture.
The Court distinguished between the executive power to notify official songs and its own duty to safeguard citizens from punitive overreach and constitutional rights violations.

explain.headline: Why Sovereign Bond Yields Are Remaining High in India
static: Sovereign bond yields represent the interest rate paid by a government to holders of its debt instruments, acting as a risk-free benchmark.
The Reserve Bank of India manages government debt and domestic liquidity using instruments like Open Market Operations (OMOs) and Variable Rate Reverse Repos (VRRR).
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) and Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) mandate commercial banks to maintain specified proportions of liquid assets.
Basel III norms regulate bank capital adequacy, market risk, and operational risk frameworks to enhance the banking sector's financial stability.
Fiscal consolidation refers to policies implemented by governments to reduce budget deficits and debt accumulation over time.

points: High long-term government bond yields have become a persistent global and domestic phenomenon despite declining inflation rates.
Domestic yields are being driven by a combination of inflation expectations, fiscal concerns, tight monetary policy, and global factors.
The core issue involves high government borrowing requirements and interest payments consuming around 37 per cent of total revenues.
Rising global crude oil prices, geopolitical tensions, and high US Treasury yields create upward pressure on domestic bond yields.
Banks are hesitant to buy government securities due to mark-to-market loss risks and tighter Basel III market-risk regulations.
Persistently high yields increase government borrowing costs, discourage private investments, and make retail loans expensive for households.
India’s strong fundamentals include core inflation remaining below 3 percent and improved liquidity following FCNR(B) mobilisation.
Policy suggestions include calibrated liquidity management by the RBI, continued fiscal consolidation, and clear policy communication.
sum.text:
Context: High bond yields have become a global phenomenon. Even though inflation has declined, long-term government bond yields remain high in countries like the US, Europe and Japan. Investors are now looking beyond inflation and focusing on high government debt, borrowing needs and risks of holding long-term bonds. In India, high bond yields are also a concern as they can increase borrowing costs, discourage private investment and affect economic growth.
Sovereign bond yield is the interest rate paid to the buyer of the bond by the government, or sovereign entity, issuing that debt instrument.
They are issued by governments to raise capital and are considered risk-free assets.
In India, high yields are being driven by a combination of inflation expectations, fiscal concerns, monetary policy expectations, liquidity conditions, market risk and global factors .
Inflation expectations: Rising global crude oil prices are creating concerns about future inflation, which encourages investors to demand higher yields on long-term government bonds.
Higher subsidy burden: The rising burden of government subsidies creates concerns about fiscal finances and future government borrowing, which can put upward pressure on bond yields.
Expectation of tight monetary policy: Markets expect monetary policy to remain relatively tight because of inflation concerns, and the hawkish tone of the August 2026 monetary-policy minutes further contributed to higher yields.
High government borrowing and interest burden: The government has significant borrowing requirements, while interest payments already consume around 37 per cent of its total revenues . Persistently high yields can therefore increase the government’s debt-servicing burden.
High US Treasury yields: Movements in US Treasury yields influence Indian bond yields because investors compare returns available in India with those available in global markets.
Geopolitical tensions: Continuing geopolitical conflicts increase uncertainty and risk premiums, which can lead investors to demand higher returns on long-term bonds.
Inadequate capital inflows: Weak net capital inflows reduce demand for Indian financial assets and can contribute to higher domestic bond yields.
Earlier tight liquidity conditions: During the second half of FY26, banks faced rapidly increasing credit demand while deposit growth remained sluggish. They therefore liquidated part of their excess Standing Liquidity Ratio and Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)…

explain.headline: UPSC Editorial Analysis: Constitutional Safeguards on Arrest and Re-Arrest
static: Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees protection of life and personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
Article 22(1) mandates that no person who is arrested shall be detained without being informed of the grounds for such arrest as soon as may be.
Article 22(1) also guarantees the right to consult and to be defended by a legal practitioner of choice.
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973 as the procedural law for criminal administration.
Over 75% of India’s prison population consists of undertrials, making procedural safeguards critical for marginalized detainees.
explain.what: The Supreme Court ruled that written communication of arrest grounds in a known language is a mandatory constitutional requirement, establishing strict checks against arbitrary re-arrests.
explain.why_in_news: The judgment in Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v. State of Punjab (2026) put the balance between personal liberty and police discretion back into focus.
explain.background: Article 22(1) and statutory provisions require informing arrested persons of their grounds of arrest, a right reinforced to prevent arbitrary detentions.
significance: Safeguards personal liberty under Article 21 and Article 22 against unchecked police powers.
Reduces the misuse of pre-trial detention and cyclic re-arrests as a form of coercive punishment.
Protects marginalized undertrials who suffer from information deficits during detentions.

Statutory baseline: Section 47 of the BNSS, 2023.
Undertrial share in Indian prisons: Over 75% according to Prison Statistics India.

texts.x: General Studies-2; Topic: Separation of powers between various organs, dispute redressal mechanisms and institutions. Introduction The Supreme Court of India (Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v. State of Punjab, 2026) reaffirmed the primacy of personal liberty over unchecked police discretion. The Court ruled that communicating the grounds of arrest in writing, in a language the accused understands, is …

points: The Supreme Court reaffirmed personal liberty over police discretion in Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v. State of Punjab, 2026.
The Court ruled that communicating arrest grounds in writing, in a language understood by the accused, is mandatory under Article 22(1).
It addressed the core dilemma of balancing citizen freedom against the state's power to investigate crimes.
Section 47 of the BNSS, 2023 requires full particulars of the offense and the right to bail to be disclosed.
Oral communication is no longer sufficient; written grounds apply universally across general and special acts like PMLA, UAPA, and NDPS.
An arrest violating Article 22(1) is void ab initio, meaning release is a termination of unlawful custody rather than bail.
Strict multi-tier rules were set for re-arrests, including magistrate approval, fresh objective grounds, superior officer consent, and officer transfers.
The judgment counters the 'process as punishment' mindset, while critics highlight operational friction and administrative burdens for police stations.
sum.text:
General Studies-2; Topic: Separation of powers between various organs, dispute redressal mechanisms and institutions.
The Supreme Court of India ( Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v. State of Punjab , 2026) reaffirmed the primacy of personal liberty over unchecked police discretion. The Court ruled that communicating the grounds of arrest in writing, in a language the accused understands, is a non-negotiable constitutional requirement under Article 22(1). It also established strict judicial checks to prevent arbitrary re-arrests.
This judgment addresses a core dilemma within India’s criminal justice system: balancing the fundamental freedom of citizens against the state’s legitimate power to investigate crime.
Article 21 (Personal Liberty): Protects life and liberty except through a “procedure established by law,” which must be fair, just, and reasonable ( Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978 ).

explain.headline: Towards a gender just Uniform Civil Code
static: Article 44 of the Directive Principles of State Policy in the Indian Constitution directs the State to secure for citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India.
Personal laws in India, governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption, have traditionally been separate for Hindus, Muslims, Christians, and Parsis based on religious customs.
The Shah Bano judgment of 1985 marked a major milestone regarding maintenance rights for Muslim women and reignited nationwide political debates on enacting a UCC.
Uttarakhand became the first state in independent India to pass and operationalize a state-level Uniform Civil Code, coming into force in January 2025.
The Hindu Code Bill enacted in the 1950s codified and reformed Hindu personal law, granting inheritance rights to women while introducing provisions like absolute property testamentary powers.

Critiques the criminalization of civil matters and the policing of live-in relationships.

points: Union Home Minister Amit Shah stated on September 13 that a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) will be implemented across all BJP- and NDA-ruled states before the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.
The author argues that while a UCC is justified through constitutional equality and gender justice, the Uttarakhand UCC conflates uniformity with equality and relies on bureaucratic hurdles.
A central concern is the mandatory registration of live-in relationships requiring notification to police and parents, which acts as surveillance rather than protection.
The Uttarakhand UCC criminalises extra-judicial dissolution of marriage with up to three years in prison and a fine, wrongly turning a civil dispute into a criminal matter.
Mandating court filing for all divorces will overwhelm already overburdened family courts, whereas customary divorces offer a speedy and economical alternative for weaker sections.
The code fails to protect women against disinheritance through wills, ignores unpaid domestic labour, and remains silent on the tax benefits of the Hindu Undivided Family.
Punitive measures like fines and imprisonment for non-registration will severely impact the poor and marginalised communities.
Justice R C Chavan resigned from the Maharashtra UCC committee on September 19, raising concerns about the lack of transparent and democratic consultations with vulnerable groups.
sum.text:
On September 13, Union Home Minister Amit Shah stated that a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) would be implemented in all 21 BJP- and NDA-ruled states before the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.
The UCC became an important goal for the BJP after the 1985 Shah Bano judgment. However, there was no draft to engage with. Then, in January 2025, Uttarakhand’s UCC came into force. Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh are awaiting Presidential assent. Maharashtra, Rajasthan, West Bengal and Chhattisgarh have set up drafting committees.
The justification for a UCC is often anchored in constitutional equality and gender justice. But a close reading of the Uttarakhand UCC reveals a law that confuses uniformity with equality and conflates regulation with protection. It has bureaucratic hurdles and criminal penalties that will disproportionately affect poor and marginalised communities. It fails to draw on progressive reforms within India’s diverse personal laws or the best practices from family codes worldwide. It ignores lived realities and legal evolution and reads like a “copy-paste” of the Hindu Code Bill, lacking vision, inclusivity, and systemic simplification.
These are some of our concerns arising from the Uttarakhand UCC, beginning with the compulsory registration of live-in relationships. Notifying police and parents is surveillance masquerading as protection. A UCC must ensure that registration, if any, is optional, confidential, and offers tangible benefits like maintenance, legitimacy of children, and inheritance rights, not social exposure. Another concern is the criminalisation of extra-judicial dissolution of marriage with three years’ punishment and a fine. Being a civil law, a UCC should avoid criminalising civil marriage disputes.
Desertion is one of the most common issues women face, leaving them and their children extremely vulnerable. A UCC should include enforceable economic remedies for deserted women, including automatic maintenance orders and injunctive relief against disposal of assets.
While the Hindu Marriage Act permits either spouse to claim maintenance, under other personal laws and the Special Marriage Act, only women can claim maintenance. A UCC should retain this gender-specific right. The deep social inequality and unequal power relations within marriage require this protection for women.
Mandating that every divorce be filed in a civil court will create a bottleneck of historic proportions. Family courts are already overburdened with lakhs of cases…

The next day, Supreme Court agreed to take up a petition questioning CEC Gyanesh Kumar's functioning and seeking to declare SIR illegal. Recent surveys point to a decline in public confidence in the fairness and legitimacy of elections. For BJP, erosion of trust in the electoral process and, by extension, in GoI, may ultimately pose a greater risk than the Opposition's resistance to SIR. Over the past year, the share of Indians who believe that elections are 'free and fair' has fallen from 64.4% to 51.9%, while the share who believe they are not, has risen from 31.7% to 40.9%. Nevertheless, they point to a deterioration in perceptions of electoral fairness. The most recent survey was conducted between July 1 and August 25, before much of the controversy surrounding EC's functioning and CEC's reported dismissal of dissent from the two other EC members came to light this month. If those developments have further affected public perceptions, the current level of confidence in the electoral process may be even lower. points: IRDAI has released a consultation paper offering reform proposals to address mis-selling in the insurance sector, with the most significant being a cap on agent, broker, and bank commissions.
The regulatory proposals caused a stock market upheaval, demonstrating how heavily insurers and banks rely on high commission revenues and highlighting the expected industry pushback.

Insurance agents typically earn upfront commissions upon sales and trail commissions annually, creating perverse incentives to push expensive endowment policies rather than consumer-friendly term covers.

Research shows customers lost around USD 28 billion to mis-sold life insurance policies between 2004 and 2011, and policy discontinuation rates remain very high with over half of policyholders quitting before five years.
Between FY23 and FY25, commissions paid through sampled corporate agents grew 2.25 times, while new business premium grew only 1.28 times.

The consultation paper proposes a tighter limit on overall expenses of management, aiming to drop insurers' expenses to 15 per cent of premium within two years and 12.5 per cent within five years from FY2027-28.
It introduces hard caps on first-year and renewal commissions across various savings, single-premium, annuity, and pure term products to reduce policy churning incentives.

The proposals crack down on mis-selling by banning banks and NBFCs from forcing borrowers to buy life insurance with loans, banning sales incentives for their staff, and introducing mandatory suitability checks.
Despite industry arguments about high customer acquisition costs and threats of shrinking sales, the author urges IRDAI not to back down, prioritizing consumer protection over market valuations.

explain.headline: Free and Fair Elections and the Controversy Surrounding the Election Commission Structure
static: Article 324 of the Indian Constitution vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections in an Election Commission consisting of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Commissioners.
Article 324(2) empowers the President to fix the number of election commissioners and states that appointments shall be subject to any law made by Parliament.

In the landmark Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023) judgment, the Supreme Court ruled that appointments must be made by a committee of the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition, and Chief Justice of India until Parliament enacted a law.

The Parliament subsequently enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, altering the selection committee composition by replacing the CJI with a Cabinet Minister.

The Kesavananda Bharati v. Union of India (1973) judgment established the basic structure doctrine, identifying democracy and free and fair elections as unalterable basic features of the Constitution.

points: On September 23rd, 2026, a Supreme Court two-judge bench referred the question of a Constitution Bench reference on the 2023 Election Commissioners Act to the Chief Justice of India.
Simultaneously, media reports revealed that the Election Commission faces internal friction, with the two Election Commissioners objecting 14 times to decisions by the Chief Election Commissioner.
The core debate centers on whether the statutory appointment mechanism under the 2023 Act compromises the institutional independence of the Election Commission of India.
The 2023 Act replaced the Chief Justice of India with a Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister in the selection committee for Election Commissioners.
Internal objections highlighted disputes over the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) excluding over 13 crore voters and unilateral amendments to Form 6.
The Election Commissioners also raised concerns about the transparency of the ECInet software and the gradual centralization of the electoral roll database.
Reports further revealed preferential treatment and quicker grievance redressal for VIP voters during the SIR process compared to ordinary citizens.
Under Section 18 of the 2023 Act, the Election Commission must decide matters unanimously or by a majority, making unilateral decisions legally questionable.
These developments indicate a trust deficit and pose serious questions regarding the constitutional integrity of India's electoral machinery.
sum.text:
“Coincidence is god’s way of staying anonymous.”.Coincidence struck on September 23rd, 2026. That morning, a two Judge bench of the Supreme Court placed before the Chief Justice of India the issue on whether a Constitution Bench reference is merited with respect to a challenge to the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 (2023 Act)..The same day, the country woke up to one of the leading newspapers having published an investigative report which unearthed that the institutional structure of the Election Commission (EC) is fractured by discontent between the Chief Election Commissioner and the other two Election Commissioners. This report revealed that in the past 10 months, the two Election Commissioners objected 14 times to the decisions taken by the Chief Election Commissioner.
These decisions were not merely administrative in nature but expressed concerns with the way the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) is being conducted by the Election Commission; the very body of which they formed an integral part. The coincidences don’t end here. The same fateful day, an online investigative journalism platform also unearthed the inner workings of the EC which have grave ramifications on the functioning of the Commission, the SIR process and the resultant effect all this has on our democracy.
None of these events bode well for our democracy..Article 324 of our Constitution deals with the ‘Election Commission’, which as per Article 324 (1) is vested with the duty to conduct all elections to the Parliament and the Legislatures. Article 324 (2) deals with the appointment of the Election Commissioner(s). As per Article 324 (2), the appointment of the Election Commissioners shall be “subject to the provisions of any law made in that behalf by Parliament…” It is noteworthy that this provision was not envisaged to be a perfunctory exercise but was supposed to be done in order to ensure that the appointment of Election Commissioner(s) is made in an independent manner; without any executive interference.
The relevance and importance of this Article can be found in the Constituent Assembly Debates. explain.headline: The United Nations’ long road to restoring trust and governance reform
static: The United Nations was established in 1945 after the Second World War under the UN Charter to maintain international peace and security.
The UN Security Council consists of 15 members: five permanent members with veto power and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.

The Uniting for Consensus (Coffee Club) is a group of countries opposing the expansion of permanent UNSC seats, advocating only for more non-permanent seats.
The Ezulwini Consensus is the African Union's common position demanding at least two permanent seats with veto power and five non-permanent seats for Africa.

points: The 81st UNGA high-level week met under the theme of restoring trust, acknowledging a deep collapse in global confidence in the UN.
Global surveys by Edelman Trust, Pew, and the UN Foundation show 52 per cent want deep structural reform and only 58 per cent trust UN leadership.
The author argues that the UN's crisis of trust stems from its governance structure, funding vulnerabilities, and accountability gaps rather than failed delivery alone.
Security Council paralysis, donor capture via voluntary extra-budgetary grants, and weak internal oversight have eroded institutional integrity.
Global South representation remains low, with developing nations holding 44 per cent of UN civil service leadership posts despite making up 84 per cent of the world's population.
The UN faces a severe liquidity crisis due to unpaid compulsory dues, deepening its dependence on earmarked funds from a few powerful donors.
Proposals to restore trust include publishing spending data to beneficiary publics, setting Global South leadership targets, and decentralising peacemaking efforts.
UNSC expansion remains stalled due to rival blocs like the G4, the Uniting for Consensus group, and the Ezulwini Consensus facing the strict amendment hurdle of Article 108.
sum.text:
The 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) held its high-level week under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: a UN that delivers for all” . The word “restoring” concedes that trust in the UN has collapsed, and global surveys confirm the fall.
Why the UN exists: Set up after the Second World War , the UN makes states’ conduct more predictable through dialogue and international law , like agreed rules in a game rivals play.
What went wrong: Over three decades, the UN went from building trust between parties in peacebuilding to needing to restore trust in itself.
Falling confidence: Edelman Trust and Pew surveys found declining trust. In a UN Foundation poll, 52 per cent want deep structural reform , saying the UN struggles to deliver.
Doubts on leadership: Only 58 per cent think the UN can lead on global problems ( Rockefeller Foundation and Focaldata poll), possibly a historic low.
The takeaway: The UN’s authority rests on states and publics trusting it, so falling trust weakens its ability to broker peace.
Security Council deadlock: UN Security Council (UNSC) paralysis eroded the Assembly’s trust, so it passed resolution A/76/262 requiring permanent members to explain each veto .

points: The author argues that the Election Commission's press note dated September 26 is a formal admission of guilt and a sound legal basis to impeach the Chief Election Commissioner and other ECs.
The ECI admitted in its note that agenda will be circulated in advance and minutes will be issued for all meetings, confirming that business was conducted without basic procedures for a year.
The press note admits to three wilful violations regarding Form 6, including misrepresenting a Supreme Court order and reverting to the original form after acknowledging earlier changes were illegal.
The ECI's plan to set up an expert committee to review ECINET is an admission that the software used to delete over 13 crore names may not comply with the law.
The press note fails to address who authorised more than 16 lakh appeals filed against voters who got their names back on rolls in Bengal.

The author contends that the Commission's actions amount to incapacity, grave dereliction of constitutional duties, and a criminal offence under Section 32(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
sum.text:
I was wrong. The exposé by The Indian Express , among the finest pieces of investigative journalism in recent times , shows that the Chief Election Commissioner could do much more than anyone had imagined. And if there was any room for doubt, the Election Commission’s own statement has officially removed it.
The ECI’s press note of September 26 is a formal admission of guilt. The two-page note is a sound legal basis to impeach the CEC. And also to remove the other two Election Commissioners who have approved this note.
Just to recap: The Constitution (Article 324(5), read with Article 124 (4)) does not allow the removal of the CEC except through impeachment on grounds of “proved misbehaviour or incapacity”. So, while impeachment does not require proving “criminality”, “misbehaviour or incapacity” does not apply to any kind of misconduct, ordinary error or a mistaken interpretation in good faith. Impeachment should kick in only in cases of gross misconduct involving the wilful breach of fundamental norms of such an office.
The Supreme Court, in Anoop Baranwal, has formulated the norms expected of the Election Commissioners. There are also the six internationally recognised “Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct”: Independence, impartiality, integrity, propriety, equality, and competence and diligence. Can anyone accuse Gyanesh Kumar of any of these virtues? In the last article, I had built a case around normative principles and substantive consequences: Blatant partisanship, impropriety and abuse of office for mass disenfranchisement. Now, we can add multiple and wilful gross violations of law to make a robust legal case against the CEC and the other ECs.
Read paragraph 1(vi) of the press note issued by the Election Commission: “For all Commission’s meeting (sic), agenda will be circulated in advance and minutes will be issued.” This is an astounding statement, especially when read in the light of The Indian Express exposé that the absence of any agenda or minutes for the past year was indeed one of the objections raised on April 16 this year by Vivek Joshi, one of the ECs. Thus, this is a formal admission that this constitutional authority has been carrying out its business without the minimum procedures required of any committee or society, or even a local club.
Unless the Commission comes out with minutes of those meetings, we must assume that there is no paper to back up the series of momentous decisions taken in the name of the Election Commission,…

points: Up to 40% of food produced in India is lost before reaching consumers, with 30-50% of perishable produce spoiling due to poor cold-chain infrastructure.
Post-harvest losses stem from inadequate storage, weak cold chains, poor handling, inefficient transportation, and fragmented supply chains with multiple intermediaries.
Low processing rates (under 10%), market gluts, excessive restaurant portions, changing urban habits, and lack of municipal waste segregation compound food waste.
The 2020-22 NABCONS study estimated post-harvest losses worth ₹26,001 crore in cereals, ₹29,545 crore in fruits, and ₹27,459 crore in vegetables.
Food loss and waste threatens food security, causes economic losses for farmers, drives food inflation, and wastes roughly 230-250 cubic kilometers of freshwater annually.
Decomposing organic waste in open landfills releases methane, with food waste accounting for 8-10% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Nutritional losses worsen India's malnutrition crisis, while total wastage imposes an estimated ₹92,000 crore to ₹1.5 lakh crore burden, hitting nearly 1% of GDP.
Government interventions include PMKSY, PM-FME, Operation Greens, Agriculture Infrastructure Fund, and FSSAI's surplus food recovery initiatives.
Mitigation strategies require expanding scientific storage, integrated cold chains, food processing, digital supply-chain technologies, and promoting circular food systems.
sum.text:
Food Loss : Up to 40% of food produced in India is lost before reaching consumers. Almost 30-50% of perishable produce like fruits & vegetables spoil due to inadequate cold chain infrastructure.
Per Capita Household Waste: The average Indian household generates about 50-55 kg of food waste per person per year, lower than the global average of 79 kg .
Inadequate storage infrastructure : Inadequate and unevenly distributed warehouses, silos, cold-storage facilities and scientific storage systems contribute significantly to post-harvest food losses in India. Perishable commodities such as fruits, vegetables, dairy and fish are particularly vulnerable to spoilage when appropriate temperature and humidity-controlled storage is unavailable. This leads to quality deterioration, distress sales, lower farmer incomes and wastage of edible food.
Weak cold-chain infrastructure : India has gaps in integrated cold-chain infrastructure connecting farms, collection centres, storage facilities, refrigerated transport and markets. Inadequate pre-cooling, insufficient refrigerated transportation and uneven distribution of cold-storage facilities can increase post-harvest spoilage and quality deterioration, leading to economic losses for farmers and reduced availability of food.
Poor post-harvest handling : Inadequate harvesting, sorting, grading, packaging and handling practices can cause physical damage, bruising and contamination of food, accelerating spoilage. Small and fragmented farms often lack access to modern post-harvest technologies, leading to significant losses.
Inefficient transportation : Inadequate transport infrastructure, long transit times, poor road connectivity and insufficient refrigerated vehicles can expose perishable food to heat, moisture and physical damage. This is particularly significant for fruits, vegetables, dairy, meat and fish, leading to spoilage before they reach markets and consumers.
Fragmented Supply Chains & Middlemen: Agricultural produce typically passes through multiple intermediaries (local traders, commission agents, regional mandis, and wholesalers) before reaching retail. Each transfer point delays delivery and increases the risk of spillage and spoilage.
Market fluctuations : Sudden changes in demand, prices and supply can make it uneconomical for farmers to harvest and transport perishable produce. During periods of market glut , excess supply of fruits and vegetables may cause prices to fall below the cost of harvesting,…

points: China is set to increase US coal imports under a September 2026 trade agreement designed to ease bilateral tensions.
The US stated China committed to buying at least 10 million tonnes of US coal annually in 2027 and 2028, though Beijing has not confirmed this volume.
The agreement puts US coal outside a framework for reciprocal tariff reductions to facilitate these imports.
China produced 4.85 billion tonnes of coal in 2025 and faces a weakening need for imports, showing the deal is not due to a shortage.
China imported about 490 million tonnes of coal and lignite last year, while the IEA expects seaborne thermal-coal imports to drop to 310 million tonnes in 2026.
US coal exports include grades like anthracite, coking coal, and bituminous coal, with high-quality coking coal used in steelmaking.
China imposed a 15% tariff on US coal in February 2025, and reducing or removing it could make US coal more competitive.
Coal provides Beijing a strategic bargaining chip to appease US President Donald Trump by narrowing the trade gap without conceding sensitive sectors.
The arrangement boosts struggling US coal miners facing a shrinking domestic market while preserving China's broader energy independence.
sum.text:
China is set to increase imports of US coal in the coming years, as Beijing and Washington look to ease tensions over trade. The move could give US coal producers greater access to the Chinese market, while giving Beijing another issue to negotiate with the US on tariffs and other trade matters.
A September 2026 agreement puts US coal outside a framework for reciprocal tariff reductions and is expected to facilitate imports to Beijing during 2027 and 2028.
US said China has committed to buying at least 10 million tonnes of US coal in each of those years, although Beijing has not confirmed that specific volume.
That gives coal an unusual role in the latest US-China trade talks. China can buy more from US producers without opening up more sensitive parts of its economy.
China produced about 4.85 billion tonnes of coal in 2025, making it the world’s largest coal producer. But its need for imports is weakening. Coal and lignite imports fell 9.6% last year to about 490 million tonnes.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects China's seaborne thermal-coal imports to fall to about 310 million tonnes in 2026, from 325 million tonnes in 2025. China has also increasingly sourced metallurgical coal from Mongolia.
The numbers suggest China is not turning to US coal because of a shortage. It already has large domestic supplies and other overseas suppliers.
The case for US coal becomes clearer when you look at the type of coal China needs.
US producers export several grades, including anthracite, coking coal and bituminous coal . Each has different uses. High-quality coking coal, for instance, is important for steelmaking.
China is the world’s largest steel producer, with crude steel output reaching nearly 1 billion tonnes in 2025, although demand for metallurgical coal is expected to dip slightly in 2026.
China’s metallurgical coal imports are forecast at around 108 million tonnes in 2026, down from an estimated 115 million tonnes in 2025. Steelmakers can blend imported coal with domestic supplies and coal from countries such as Mongolia, Australia and Canada to secure the quality they need.
China needs coal in steelmaking mainly because coking coal is converted into coke, which provides the high heat needed to melt iron ore in blast furnaces. Coke also acts as a reducing agent, removing oxygen from iron ore to produce molten iron.
Although China is the world’s largest steel producer, it still imports coking coal to secure the specific grades and quality required…

points: India's Essar Group is planning an $18 billion steel plant and mining project in the US through its subsidiary Mesabi Metallics.
The major investment is driven by the Trump administration's 50% tariff on imported foreign steel, which incentivizes domestic manufacturing.
The project features a fully integrated supply chain connecting an iron-ore mine in Minnesota to a proposed steel plant in Iowa.
The Iowa steel facility is expected to cost about $15 billion, while the Minnesota iron-ore mine investment accounts for about $3 billion.
US President Donald Trump announced the project, noting it will create thousands of construction, manufacturing, and mining jobs.
Production at the Iowa facility is slated to begin around 2030, with initial output planned at 7.5 million tonnes before reaching 10 million tonnes annually.
The Minnesota mine is described as the first new iron-ore mine opened in the US in more than 50 years.
Essar acquired the Minnesota operations originally known as Minnesota Steel in 2007 through Mesabi Metallics, securing large iron-ore resources.
sum.text:
India's Essar Group is making an $18 billion bet on the US steel industry, with its subsidiary Mesabi Metallics planning a large steel plant in Iowa linked to an iron-ore mine in Minnesota .
The project was announced by US President Donald Trump on Monday. The Iowa facility is expected to produce up to 10 million tonnes of steel annually once fully operational, while the broader project is expected to create thousands of jobs. Production is expected to begin around 2030.
But why is an Indian conglomerate putting billions of dollars into US steel production? Trump's 50% tariffs on imported steel are a key part of the answer offered by the administration and Essar executives.
The investment is structured around a fully integrated US supply chain, linking Mesabi Metallics' iron-ore operation in Minnesota to the proposed Iowa steel plant.
Rewant Ruia, chairman of Mesabi Metallics, said his family was investing about $3 billion in the Minnesota iron-ore mine and described the broader plan as a supply chain "from mine to mill".
The Iowa plant is expected to receive iron ore from the Minnesota operation, allowing the company to mine the raw material and manufacture steel within the US.
The steel plant itself is expected to account for about $15 billion of the project, with the broader investment taking the total to approximately $18 billion.
The Trump administration has imposed a 50% tariff on foreign steel, raising the cost of exporting steel into the US.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the tariffs were central to the investment, stating that without them, "this mine doesn’t get built, and this steel plant does not get built".
Trump similarly said companies were building in the US "because they don’t want to pay tariffs".
The investment therefore illustrates how the tariff regime is intended to encourage companies to manufacture inside the US rather than export steel into the American market.
The Iowa facility is planned to produce up to 10 million tonnes of steel a year once fully built out, which would make it the largest steel plant in the US, according to the White House and company plans.
The first phase is expected to begin production around 2030. Reuters reported that initial production is planned at about 7.5 million tonnes annually before the facility reaches its full capacity.

points: The Commission for Air Quality Management approved a revised Graded Response Action Plan schedule during its 30th full commission meeting.
The revision formalises earlier ad-hoc orders by embedding stricter pollution-control measures directly into the permanent GRAP framework.
Exemptions for BS-IV and below goods vehicles carrying essential commodities have been removed under Stages III and IV.
The revised schedule now features a total of 48 actions across four distinct stages of air quality severity.
Actions concerning diesel generator sets and the entry of BS-IV and below buses from adjoining states were shifted from Stage II to Stage I.

sum.text:
Older goods vehicles carrying essential commodities will no longer be exempt from curbs once the two strictest stages of Delhi-NCR’s pollution-control plan kick in. The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) has removed the exemption for BS-IV and below vehicles under Stages III and IV of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).
The change is part of a revised GRAP schedule approved by the CAQM Full Commission at its meeting on Monday. It removes the exemption for light and medium goods vehicles (LGVs and MGVs) at Stage III, and for trucks and heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) at Stage IV.
To be sure, similar curbs have been in place before. The commission had imposed them through separate orders issued on top of GRAP last year.
“We had issued orders on top of the existing GRAP restrictions earlier. But now we have formalised these restrictions by including them in GRAP,” an official aware of the matter said. “State governments can refer to these and are also welcome to implement directions beyond these as well.”
One such order restricts older goods vehicles entering Delhi throughout the year. In October 2025, CAQM amended one of its directions and under it, commercial goods vehicles registered outside Delhi were barred from entering the city since November 1, 2025 unless they are BS-VI, CNG, LNG or electric. BS-III and below vehicles were shut out whatever they carried. BS-IV vehicles got a one-year transitional window, which ends on October 31, 2026.
The revised GRAP also spells out, under Stage III, the restriction on entry into Delhi of diesel BS-IV and below LGVs and MGVs registered outside the city.
Addressing a press conference, CAQM member-technical Dr SD Attri said the revised schedule has 48 actions across the four stages: 25 under Stage I, eight under Stage II, 10 under Stage III and five under Stage IV.
Actions related to diesel generator sets, and to the entry of BS-IV and below buses from NCR and adjoining states, have moved from Stage II to Stage I, so they apply at an earlier stage of pollution.
Restrictions on plying BS-III petrol and BS-IV diesel four-wheelers have been extended to Sonipat. They already apply in the high vehicle density districts of Gurugram, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Gautam Budh Nagar.
The schedule merges repeated Stage I measures on dust control, municipal solid waste management and transport. It also allows a minor relaxation under the first Stage III action, including for repairing potholes.

The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Friday approved the Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojana Rasayan (BHAVYA Rasayan) scheme for the establishment of three dedicated chemical parks across the country, aiming to strengthen India’s chemical manufacturing ecosystem, attract investments and enhance global competitiveness.
The scheme, announced in the Union Budget for 2026-27, has a total financial outlay of ₹3,030 crore, including ₹3,000 crore for developing common infrastructure facilities and basic utilities within the parks and ₹30 crore towards administrative expenses. The scheme will be implemented over five years, from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31.
Under the scheme, the Centre will provide financial assistance of up to ₹1,000 crore for each chemical park, subject to a minimum contribution of ₹500 crore by the respective state government.
The chemical parks will be developed by state governments through a challenge-based selection process, with each park requiring at least 2,000 acres (8 sq. km.) of contiguous, encumbrance-free land.
According to the government, the scheme is designed to promote the development of the chemical industry across the entire value chain, including upstream, downstream and ancillary industries, while improving resource efficiency and reducing logistics costs.
The parks will feature plug-and-play infrastructure tailored to the needs of the chemical sector, including Common Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs), Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facilities (TSDFs), water supply and distribution systems, solvent recovery and distillation facilities, steam generation and distribution networks, interconnected pipeline systems, and logistics and warehousing infrastructure.
The government said shared infrastructure would improve cost competitiveness for domestic manufacturers, helping the Indian chemical industry integrate more effectively into global value chains, increase exports and reduce import dependence.
The scheme also aims to promote environmentally sustainable industrial development through centralised waste treatment, hazardous waste management and compliance infrastructure, enabling industries to meet environmental regulations more efficiently.

sum.text:
The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Thursday approved the GOBARdhan (Galvanizing Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan) National Circular Bioenergy Scheme with a total outlay of ₹23,731 crore. The scheme aims to transform India’s vast organic waste resources into clean energy, rural livelihoods and economic growth.
In a post on X, PM Modi said, “A vital step towards clean energy, rural prosperity and realising our collective dream of an Atmanirbhar Bharat! The Cabinet has approved GOBARdhan Scheme, which will give a major boost to Compressed Biogas, with the aim of increasing domestic CBG production nearly ten-fold. The scheme will create a strong and predictable ecosystem for investment and innovation. It will benefit our farmers, cooperatives, MSMEs, women entrepreneurs and rural enterprises while strengthening energy security, reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels and promoting scientific waste management.”
The scheme, to be implemented from FY 2026-27 to FY 2035-36, seeks to establish Compressed Biogas (CBG) as a major component of India’s future energy mix by creating an integrated framework that provides assured demand, stable pricing, capital assistance, pipeline connectivity, credit support and technology development.
The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas said that the initiative is expected to increase domestic CBG production by nearly ten times, strengthen India’s energy security, attract large-scale private investment and accelerate the transition towards a circular bioeconomy.
The scheme aims to convert agricultural residue, cattle dung, press mud, municipal organic waste and other biomass resources into renewable fuel, organic manure and additional income for farmers while promoting sustainable waste management across the country.
The Ministry will implement the scheme, bringing together various elements of the compressed biogas value chain under a single national framework to improve project viability and provide greater certainty to investors, lenders and developers.
The Ministry said the initiative builds on the foundation laid through earlier programmes such as the Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation (SATAT) initiative, the Market Development Assistance (MDA) scheme for organic manure, the Biomass Aggregation Machinery (BAM) scheme, the Development of Pipeline Infrastructure (DPI) scheme and financial assistance provided under the National Bioenergy Programme.

The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Friday approved the continuation of the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN) scheme for the period 2026-27 to 2030-31, with a financial outlay of ₹3.15 lakh crore. The decision aims to ensure continued income support to eligible farmer families through the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) system.
In a post on X, PM Modi said, “We are committed to empowering and ensuring the prosperity of our farmer brothers and sisters across the country. In line with this commitment, approval has been granted today to extend the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN) scheme until 2030-31. The scheme not only helps our annadatas (food providers) meet expenses related to seeds, fertilisers and other agricultural needs, but is also improving their overall financial well-being.”
Launched in February 2019, the PM-KISAN scheme provides ₹6,000 annually to eligible landholding farmer families in three equal instalments, transferred directly into their bank accounts. The government said the scheme has emerged as a transparent and technology-driven model of farmer welfare through Aadhaar-based authentication, digital verification and the DBT mechanism.
Since its launch, more than ₹4.47 lakh crore has been transferred directly into the bank accounts of farmers through 23 instalments. Under the 23rd instalment, over 9.49 crore farmers received financial assistance amounting to more than ₹18,984 crore. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the scheme disbursed over ₹1.71 lakh crore to support farmers. Women beneficiaries have received more than ₹1.06 lakh crore under the scheme, with nearly one in every four beneficiaries being a woman farmer.
According to the government, the financial assistance provided under PM-KISAN has enabled farmers to make timely investments in seeds, fertilisers, irrigation, farm machinery and other agricultural inputs, while reducing dependence on informal sources of credit and improving the financial stability of rural households.

static: Preventive detention involves detaining a person to prevent them from committing future crimes, rather than punishing them for a past crime.
The National Security Act (NSA), 1980 empowers the Central and State governments to detain individuals to prevent them from acting in a manner prejudicial to national security or public order.
Under the NSA, an individual can be detained without charges for up to 12 months, though the grounds must be communicated and advisory boards must review the case.
Article 22 of the Constitution provides safeguards against arbitrary arrest and detention, though preventive detention laws are an explicit exception.
Judicial review remains a vital safeguard against the misuse of preventive detention powers by executive authorities.

explain.background: Preventive detention laws like the National Security Act allow authorities to detain individuals without trial to prevent future acts, subject to constitutional safeguards and judicial review.
significance: Reiterates strict judicial scrutiny over the executive's use of stringent preventive detention laws.
Clarifies that custodial confessional statements cannot serve as the sole basis for subjective satisfaction under the NSA.
Highlights the importance of considering surrounding circumstances and relevant material before depriving an individual of liberty.

points: The Supreme Court quashed the National Security Act detention of Mulla Afroz, accused of masterminding the 2024 Sambhal violence.
The trigger was an appeal filed by Afroz against the Allahabad High Court judgment that had upheld his preventive detention.
The core issue debated was whether an alleged confessional statement made in police custody can form the sole ground for preventive detention.
A Bench comprising Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Sheel Nagu held that an alleged confession cannot be the sole ground for detention.
The Court ruled that surrounding circumstances must be looked into and found that the detaining authority failed to consider appropriate material.
The Supreme Court concluded that the power of detention had been illegally exercised by the authorities.
The Court set aside the detention order, the confirmation order, and the Allahabad High Court judgment upholding the detention.
The Court additionally imposed costs of ₹10 lakh on the State of Uttar Pradesh for the illegal detention.
sum.text:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday quashed the National Security Act (NSA) detention of Mulla Afroz, accused of being the alleged mastermind of the 2024 Sambhal violence [Mulla Afroz v. Union of India & Ors.]..A Bench of Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Sheel Nagu held that an alleged confessional statement cannot be the sole ground for preventive detention. "Confessional statement cannot be the sole ground for detention, surrounding circumstances have to be looked into," said the Court.
The Court found that the detaining authority had failed to take into consideration appropriate material before passing the detention order.“In fact, whatever has been said by the detaining authority has been discussed to hold that the power of detention has been illegally exercised,” it said. The Court accordingly allowed Afroz's appeal and quashed the detention order, the confirmation order and the Allahabad High Court judgment upholding his detention. Additionally, it also imposed costs of ₹10 lakh on the State of Uttar Pradesh..The case arose from the violence that broke out in Sambhal in November 2024, following a court-ordered survey of the Shahi Jama Masjid.
Four people were killed in the violence. Afroz was arrested around 54 days after the incident and was subsequently granted bail by the Allahabad High Court. The Sambhal District Magistrate, however, passed an order on October 13, 2025 directing Afroz's preventive detention under Section 3 of the NSA.
The order was subsequently upheld by the Allahabad High Court, following which Afroz approached the Supreme Court. Before the Supreme Court, Afroz challenged the material relied upon for his detention, including an alleged confessional statement made in police custody. The Court questioned the State on whether such a confession could form the basis of the detaining authority's satisfaction under the NSA..[Read Live Coverage]

sum.text:
Union Home Minister Amit Shah unveiled PRAHAAR, which stands for Policy for Response Against Hostile Activities and Radicalism, as India’s first national counter-terrorism policy and strategy on 23 February 2026. A conference on “PRAHAAR – CT Policy and Strategy” was held in New Delhi on 28 September 2026, and the strategy was discussed as a 10-year institutional framework.
PRAHAAR is a multi-dimensional counter-terrorism strategy built on seven pillars. These pillars are Prevention, Response, Aggregating Internal Capacities, Human Rights, Attenuating Conditions for Terrorism, Aligning International Efforts, and Recovery and Resilience.
The framework uses a whole-of-society approach and includes social, psychological, and community-based measures for preventing radicalisation. The strategy also places emphasis on zero tolerance for terror and on implementation up to the police station level.
During the 28 September 2026 conference, the need for an automated counter-terrorism response at every level was discussed. The conference was attended by the Union Home Secretary, Foreign Secretary, heads of Central Armed Police Forces, heads of Central Police Organisations, Directors General of Police of 15 states, and Anti-Terrorist Squad chiefs of all states and Union Territories.
An Extradition Portal was also launched on 28 September 2026 to coordinate and speed up efforts to bring fugitives back to India. From 2019 to 2026, 288 fugitive criminals were repatriated to India from 36 countries.
More than 40 modules of the Shahzad Bhatti network were busted through improved agency coordination. The network was linked to cross-border smuggling of weapons, explosives, and narcotics, and more than 100 FIRs and 350 arrests were recorded across 15 states. The network was also declared a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.

points: The Reserve Bank of India has soaked up an estimated $20 billion of excess rupee liquidity through foreign exchange operations.
The central bank utilized dollar-rupee sell-buy swaps, spot dollar sales, bond sales, and variable-rate reverse repos to manage liquidity.
These liquidity tightening measures combined with seasonal tax outflows have more than halved the banking system's liquidity surplus.
The banking system's liquidity surplus had previously touched a record 11.16 trillion rupees in the first week of September.
Core liquidity dropped significantly from a peak of 14.2 trillion rupees on September 4 to 11.5 trillion rupees.
Economists estimate that net RBI dollar sales of about $18.5 billion through spot transactions and swaps drove the core liquidity decline.
The RBI's sell-buy swaps pushed dollar-rupee forward premiums higher, raising hedging costs with the one-year premium up around 50 basis points.

sum.text:
MUMBAI, Sept 29 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of India's foreign exchange operations have soaked up an estimated $20 billion of excess rupee liquidity, two bankers said, with dollar-rupee swaps playing a prominent role in liquidity management.
The RBI has used a combination of dollar-rupee sell-buy swaps, spot dollar sales, bond sales and variable-rate reverse repos in recent weeks to drain excess liquidity from the banking system.
Those measures, along with tax outflows, have more than halved the banking system's liquidity surplus from a record 11.16 trillion rupees ($116.10 billion) in the first week of the month.
Economists have said the decline was evident in core liquidity, which strips out daily swings in cash balances to show the more persistent surplus.
Core liquidity fell to 11.5 trillion rupees from a peak of 14.2 trillion rupees on September 4, according to Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at IDFC First Bank.
RBI net dollar sales of about $18.5 billion through spot transactions and sell-buy swaps, along with bond sales, drove the decline, she estimated.
"We estimate another 1.5 trillion rupees of liquidity may be removed via bond sales and sell-buy FX swaps," Sengupta said.
Economists said the nearly $20 billion drained through FX operations was the net impact, with actual dollar sales through spot transactions and sell-buy swaps likely higher.
FX swaps are becoming an increasingly important liquidity tool for the RBI, a senior treasury official at a foreign bank said, declining to be identified because he was not authorised to speak to the media.
The RBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The central bank's sell/buy swaps have pushed dollar-rupee forward premiums higher, raising the cost of hedging dollar exposure, with the one-year premium up around 50 basis points this month.
The RBI had signaled it would use these tools, with Governor Sanjay Malhotra saying the central bank had several ways to drain surplus liquidity, including bond sales and FX swaps.
Malhotra had noted that the RBI waived cash reserve requirements on FCNR(B) deposits, suggesting a broad CRR increase was not its preferred option.
"The RBI is simultaneously calibrating liquidity while shielding the economy from potentially disruptive shocks," said Tanay Dalal, senior vice president of business and economic research at Axis Bank.
(Reporting by Nimesh Vora, additional reporting by Dharamraj Dhutia; Editing by Nivedita Bhattacharjee)

Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh called the move an “astonishing U-turn” and alleged that the government was pushing ahead with a project that could cause serious ecological damage.

Ramesh shared a screenshot of a media report about the Centre’s move and alleged that the government had been pushing the project despite concerns over its environmental and forest-related approvals.
“The Modi Govt has been bulldozing through the Rs 92,000 crore (revised upward from the earlier Rs 72,000 crore) Great Nicobar Island Project. One of these petitions deals with alleged violations of the Forest Rights Act, 2006, and concerns the rights of local tribal communities, he said. The final hearing in the matter is scheduled for November 25 and 26, 2026, according to Ramesh.

New Delhi [India], September 29 (ANI): The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) and the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) have signed an MoU to strengthen the Statistical Business Register (SBR), as per a statement by the Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises on Tuesday. The MoU sets the terms and understanding between both the ministries regarding the sharing of unit-wise data of the Udyam Registration available with the MSME Department through APIs. Also, the two-way API shall provide data for preparation of the National Statistical Business Register (NSBR), as per the release shared by the MSME Ministry.“A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) has been exchanged between the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises and the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), to institutionalise a mechanism for sharing relevant data for the development and strengthening of the Statistical Business Register (SBR),” the Ministry said in the release.
It further noted that the MOU will facilitate a structured framework for sharing relevant information from the Udyam Registration ecosystem of the Ministry of MSME with MoSPI. “The information will contribute to improving the coverage, consistency and reliability of business information used for statistical purposes,” the Ministry said. The Statistical Business Register (SBR) is a centralised and regularly updated database of registered businesses, enterprises, establishments and other economic units operating within a defined geographical area.
It records key characteristics of these economic units and the relationships between them, providing a common framework for compiling business-related information. The SBR forms are a key part of the economic statistics system by improving the coverage, consistency and reliability of business data. It helps identify target populations and select samples for economic surveys, supports the compilation of business demography statistics, and enables better integration of data from different sources.
The MoU was signed by Rajneesh, Additional Secretary & Development Commissioner, Ministry of MSME and Dalip Singh, Additional Director General, MoSPI. sum.text:
New Delhi: Ten of the 19 sub-sectors tracked by India's new Index of Services Production (ISP) recorded double-digit growth in July 2026 from a year earlier, while seven others also expanded, signalling sustained momentum in formal-sector services despite mixed signals from manufacturing and external trade.
The data were part of the fourth trial release of the ISP, unveiled by the government on Tuesday with 2024-25 as the base year. The index marks a significant overhaul of India's economic statistics and provides policymakers with a long-awaited monthly measure of activity in the services sector, which accounts for more than half of the economy.
The 19 sectors account for about 60% of the services economy. The single composite ISP will be released later, after assessing the stability and resilience of the sub-sectoral indices and improving their coverage, the ministry of statistics and programme implementation ( MoSPI ) said in a statement.
The monthly series is expected to improve short-term gross domestic product (GDP) forecasting, help the central bank better gauge demand conditions while framing monetary policy and provide businesses with an additional tool to monitor sectoral trends.
Top sub-sectors reporting continued strong growth in July include accommodation and food (12.6%), retail trade (18.5%), administrative and support services (20.9%), Banking (12.3%), wholesale trade (12.1%) and real estate (14.4%).
Air transport services contracted 8.4% from a year earlier in July as the West Asia conflict drove energy prices higher. Repair services also contracted, shrinking 5% during the month. Postal and courier as well as and information and broadcasting services that were in the negative zone in earlier months expanded by 8.7% and 10%, respectively, in July.
According to the MoSPI data, rail transport growth recovered in July, expanding 7.5% while road transport services grew by 9.9% and water transport by 7.7%. The wholesale trade grew by 7.7% during the month. Telecommunication, banking and insurance sectors expanded by 11%, 12.3% and 8.9%, respectively.
In July, information technology (IT) and computer-related services grew by 10.7%, professional, scientific and technical services, including research and development, expanded by 10.4%, administrative and support services by 20.9% and arts, entertainment and recreation services by 1.7%.

static: A curative petition is the last constitutional resort available in the Supreme Court against a final judgment, entertained only under extraordinary circumstances to prevent abuse of process or miscarriage of justice.

sum.text:
A curative plea has been filed before the Supreme Court seeking recall of its September 23 split verdict on whether challenges to the law governing the appointment of Election Commissioners should be referred to a larger bench. The plea, filed by Dr Jaya Thakur, alleges a conflict of interest involving Justice Satish Chandra Sharma, who had favoured referring the matter to a larger five-judge Constitution Bench. Thakur’s plea states that Justice Sharma’s son, Siddharth Sharma, has been a standing counsel for the Election Commission of India before the Madhya Pradesh High Court since July 2024.
The plea argues that this created a “reasonable apprehension of bias and propriety” and that Justice Sharma should have disclosed his son’s role and engagement with the ECI before hearing the case. It seeks a fresh hearing and contends that Justice Sharma should not have heard the matter because of the alleged conflict of interest. Bar and Bench reported the filing on Tuesday.
What was the September 23 split verdict? On September 23, a two-judge bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma delivered separate opinions on the Centre’s request to refer petitions challenging the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 to a larger bench. Justice Datta rejected the Centre’s request for a larger-bench reference, while Justice Sharma favoured referring the matter to a Constitution Bench.
The two judges, however, agreed that the matter should be placed before the Chief Justice of India for consideration of a bench of appropriate strength, rather than sending it through the usual route to a three-judge bench, which they said could delay the proceedings. The petitions challenge provisions of the 2023 law governing the appointment of the CEC and Election Commissioners. Under the law, the selection committee comprises the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister.
What does the curative plea allege? According to the plea, Thakur learnt about Siddharth Sharma’s engagement as counsel for the ECI only after media reports on September 25. It argues that Siddharth Sharma’s professional role representing the ECI and Justice Sharma’s adjudication of a case challenging the law governing the appointment of Election Commissioners created a conflict that warranted disclosure.

Five new sites and serial and transnational proposals have been included in India’s UNESCO Tentative List, increasing India’s count to 78. New Delhi, Sep 29 (PTI) In a scathing observation, the Supreme Court on Tuesday said that most states tend not to follow the judgment in the Prakash Singh case aimed at having DGPs of their choosing.
The observation was made by a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana while reserving its order on pleas challenging the process followed by the Odisha government in selecting candidates for appointment of the state's director general of police (DGP).
On September 24, the bench asked the Odisha government if it had put a senior IPS officer, whose name was excluded from a list of officers being considered for the DGP's post, in the category of accused after the CBI stated that he might need to be questioned in a recruitment exam scam case.
While reserving the verdict, the CJI said that the bench would see whether the appointment of the DGP in Odisha and Jharkhand was made according to the directions issued by the apex court in the Prakash Singh judgment.
"The state would like to derail the appointment process and do not want to follow the Prakash Singh (judgment)... they want to have the DGP of their choice," the CJI said.
The top court also came down heavily on the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), which was tasked by it to shortlist three names of senior Indian Police Service (IPS) officers amongst the list provided by states for appointment as the DGP, for its casual approach.
"The casual approach is reflected everywhere, and you are in a position of trust conferred by this court. First of all, it is very difficult to reconcile the composition of the (UPSC) committee itself. This is all just an eyewash.
"The appointment of DGPs is governed by judicial orders of this court. Every state has to satisfy us that the appointment is in accordance with the orders of this court…," the CJI said.

sum.text:
The Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) announced five digital identity initiatives at Aadhaar Samvaad in Kolkata on 29 September 2026, which marked the 17th Aadhaar Day. The initiatives cover Aadhaar authentication, resident services, and digital governance under the Aadhaar ecosystem.
Face Authentication for the Electronic Public Distribution System (ePDS) is one of the new launches. The system is a joint initiative of UIDAI, the Department of Food and Public Distribution, and the National Informatics Centre. The ePDS is a digital platform used for public distribution of subsidised food grains in India.
UIDAI introduced SWIK Portal 2.0 for non-Government entities that seek approval for Aadhaar authentication under the Aadhaar Authentication for Good Governance framework. The new Sub-AUA/Sub-KUA (LITE) Framework is designed for government and eligible non-government entities with low-volume authentication requirements. A Sub-AUA is a Sub Authentication User Agency, and a Sub-KUA is a Sub KYC User Agency in the Aadhaar authentication architecture.
UIDAI launched a new Token Management System for individuals visiting UIDAI state and regional offices for services. The UIDAI website has also been revamped and now supports 13 languages, with a planned expansion to 23 languages. The website includes a career portal for online applications for deputation opportunities.

Jaipur, Sep 29 The Rajasthan High Court has expressed serious concern over the threat to the UNESCO World Heritage status of Jaipur's Walled City (Char Diwari). Taking suo motu cognisance of the issue, Justice Pramil Kumar Mathur directed that the matter be placed before the Chief Justice for registration as a Public Interest Litigation (PIL). The Court noted that four World Heritage Sites across the world have already lost their UNESCO status and warned that Jaipur could become the fifth if timely corrective measures are not taken.
It observed that the UNESCO World Heritage Committee had previously raised concerns over the demolition of historic buildings within Jaipur's Walled City and the inadequate implementation of heritage conservation regulations. According to the Court, UNESCO had raised concerns as early as 2023. It observed that effective measures had not been taken and said that corrective action would be necessary before December 2026 to prevent any threat to Jaipur's World Heritage status.
In its order, the Court said illegal construction, unauthorised alterations and widespread encroachments in the core and buffer zones of the Walled City posed a serious threat to its heritage character. The Court noted that several buildings had allegedly been altered or demolished in violation of the Heritage Conservation and Protection Regulations, 2020, which were framed to safeguard historic structures. The Court also questioned the functioning of officials of the Jaipur Municipal Corporation and Jaipur Development Authority (JDA), observing that the agencies had failed to effectively implement applicable laws and policies.
It further expressed concern over the lack of coordination among government departments, describing the situation as reflecting systemic apathy and negligence. The Court observed that traditional havelis and other heritage structures were gradually disappearing and being replaced by modern buildings that did not harmonise with the historical character of the Walled City. The order also highlighted other issues affecting the heritage character of the area, including tangled networks of overhead wires visible at several locations within the Walled City.

sum.text:
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Tuesday approved the revised capital cost of ₹3,630.77 crore for the construction of a Greenfield connectivity corridor linking the Noida International Airport to the Delhi-Mumbai Expressway.
The 31.42 km-long project, to be developed under the Hybrid Annuity Mode (HAM), will connect the airport with the Delhi-Faridabad-Ballabhgarh-Sohna spur of the expressway. The project will be implemented across the states of Uttar Pradesh and Haryana.
According to the CCEA, the corridor will provide direct and high-speed connectivity from South Delhi, Faridabad and Gurugram to the upcoming airport, improving access and boosting logistics efficiency across the National Capital Region.
The proposed route will intersect with major transport corridors including the Eastern Peripheral Expressway, the Yamuna Expressway and the Dedicated Freight Corridor, enabling greater multimodal connectivity in the region.
The CCEA said that around 11 km of the project will be developed as an elevated highway, forming a key segment of the Greenfield corridor linking the DND-Ballabhgarh Bypass to Jewar International Airport and further connecting it with the Delhi-Mumbai Expressway.
The elevated section is expected to support future urban expansion under the Faridabad Master Plan 2031 and accommodate planned high-density development in the region. The additional cost of the elevated stretch has been estimated at ₹689.24 crore, of which the Government of Haryana has agreed to contribute ₹450 crore.
The CCEA said the project will play a critical role in unlocking the economic potential of the Jewar Airport-Delhi-Mumbai Expressway corridor, while also strengthening regional connectivity and supporting sustainable urban development in Faridabad and surrounding areas.
